apocryphal

/uh-POK-ruh-ful/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Apocryphal means of doubtful authenticity, widely circulated but almost certainly untrue, though often retold as if true.

The tale that the young general wept because there were no more worlds to conquer is probably apocryphal, but writers have retold it for centuries.

Worked Example

Every summer, tour guides in the harbor town repeat the story that a celebrated novelist wrote her most famous chapter in a single afternoon at the corner cafe. A local historian finally checked ship manifests, hotel registers, and the novelist's own letters, and found she had never visited the town at all. The cafe keeps its brass plaque anyway. The story is apocryphal: widely retold, fondly believed, and almost certainly untrue.

The cafe story is a charming tale that people keep retelling in good faith even though the evidence shows it almost certainly never happened, which is exactly what apocryphal means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dubious: Dubious means of doubtful truth or reliability - a dubious claim invites suspicion but the verdict is still open. Apocryphal is more specific and more settled: it describes a story that is almost certainly untrue yet keeps circulating because people enjoy retelling it. A dubious rumor awaits judgment; an apocryphal legend has survived it.

unverified: Unverified means no one has confirmed the claim yet - the checking simply has not been done, so the truth is still open. Apocryphal goes further: the story has been examined, is almost certainly untrue, and circulates anyway. An unverified report awaits evidence; an apocryphal tale has outlived the evidence against it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

authentic: genuine and verified as real

documented: supported by reliable written evidence

Where it sits · how far the story strays from truth — embellished → apocryphal → fabricated

embellished vs. apocryphal: An embellished account stretches real events with extra flourishes, while an apocryphal one is almost certainly not true at all, no matter how often it is retold.

fabricated vs. apocryphal: An apocryphal legend grows up innocently around something people want to believe, but a fabricated story is invented outright, usually with the intent to deceive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — apo-

Prefix — apo-: away, off (Greek)

Root — cryph

Root — cryph: from Greek kryptein, to hide

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of, having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Apocryphal combines Greek apo-, 'away,' with kryptein, 'to hide,' plus the suffix -al, 'characteristic of.' The Apocrypha were writings 'hidden away' outside the accepted biblical canon because their authorship was doubted, so apocryphal came to mean characteristic of those hidden texts: of doubtful authenticity.

Use the root in a new word: crypt

Use the root in a new word: crypt: The abbey's crypt, a burial chamber hidden beneath the main floor, takes its name from the same Greek root kryptein, 'to hide.'

Word Choice

literary, journalistic register

Apocryphal attaches to stories, quotations, and origin tales (an apocryphal anecdote, an apocryphal deathbed quip). It implies a legend retold in good faith because people enjoy believing it, which sets it apart from a plain lie told to deceive.
